segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: When he was in his 20s-- it was years ago-- Pablo Torre started appearing on TV, talking about sports, talking about something that now he's kind of embarrassed about.

segments.speaker: Pablo Torre
segments.text: I was a gasbag on ESPN. Various people did not like me, I think. I just sort of represented this new young person who was vaguely Asian but also Mexican. I'm Filipino. That answers that mystery.

segments.speaker: Pablo Torre
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Pablo Torre
segments.text: But I had this take from the very beginning of my time on TV back in 2012, which was, we debate in sports all of the time. How much did the refs blow this? What should the call have been? Who's the hero? Who's the villain? What's right, and what's wrong? And I had been arguing forever that robots can solve this. Like, we have the technology. If you replace the referee or the umpire with a robot, we don't need to waste our time arguing about this dumb shit.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And so that became your stance.

segments.speaker: Pablo Torre
segments.text: It became a thing I was known for, was calling for this robot referee revolution. Like, the guy won't shut up about these robots.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: He winces now when he thinks about it.

segments.speaker: Pablo Torre
segments.text: Anyhow, years go on. And then finally, in 2021, I see this story break that, at long last, the most traditional sport in all of America, Major League Baseball, is experimenting with robot umpires in the minor leagues.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Minor league teams installed what they called the ABS system, the Automated Ball Strike system, these hawkeye cameras with optical tracking. They looked out over home plate and saw perfectly whether every pitch was in the strike zone and then told the human umpire, who was standing there, through an earpiece, whether to call it a ball or strike.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And the way it worked in the early versions is that the robots made the call, and the human umpire just let the fans and players know what the robot said. Pablo got what he always dreamed of, what he'd always pontificated about. There was no more need to argue about the umpire's calls, no more reason to boo the umpire from the stands. And? When Pablo watched those games?

segments.speaker: Pablo Torre
segments.text: It wasn't as good. It wasn't as good. Because so much of what going to a baseball game is like is you sitting in the stands and effectively using the airspace around you as this sort of pillow you can scream into, releasing whatever it is pent up over the course of your day and your week and, frankly, your childhood. And you're getting to unleash it on-- and this is, I think, a really important part of this-- on another person.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Pablo says that watching the minor league games, knowing that the human umpire was just the messenger for the robot empire and its perfect calls of balls and strikes--

segments.speaker: Pablo Torre
segments.text: It felt like the equivalent of talking to a customer service rep that you know isn't a person. It's like, I get that you're making human noises, but it's eerie. And then realizing, oh, no, no-- I want a human. Because when you're getting mad at an umpire in these minor league, full ABS system games, you're just yelling at your computer monitor.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Then this season-- I'm guessing a lot of you have heard this-- the robot umpires arrived in the major leagues. The ABS system went into every Major League Baseball park. And every game in those parks has used that technology. And the problem that Pablo had with ABS when he first saw it in the minors-- they fixed it. They fixed it completely and fully with a competence he had never expected from Major League Baseball. How'd they do it?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So explain for people who aren't watching baseball how the system works now.

segments.speaker: Pablo Torre
segments.text: It's brilliant, the way it works now, and I didn't see it coming. The way it works is that it's not a computer telling the umpire in their ear, this is a ball, and this is a strike. What's happening instead is the umpire, the human being, is going about their job as they have for decades upon decades.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So the umpire is calling the game, the way they always have.

segments.speaker: Pablo Torre
segments.text: Yes, except now there is a challenge system, in which the batter, the pitcher, the catcher, they can basically throw a flag and say, in so many words, I think the umpire messed up. And at that point, the robot, up on the jumbotron, they show you whether the umpire actually got it right or wrong. And what it did was, in this brilliant way, once again, we are judging a human being, the umpire.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So to show just how satisfying that can be for fans, this is a game in Cincinnati in March. It's the Reds versus the Boston Red Sox. This is only three days after they started doing these challenges. Ryan Watson is pitching for Boston, and this is actually his very first game pitching Major League Baseball. And then in the sixth inning, Boston is behind 5 to 3. Cincinnati is at bat. Bases are loaded. They have two outs.

segments.speaker: Commentator
segments.text: A Red at every base, with two down.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: A player named Eugenio Suárez is at bat.

segments.speaker: Commentator
segments.text: They're paying him to hit the ball out of the ballpark. This is certainly the moment of the game to this point. Here comes the 1-2. And in there! Struck him out! Now they're going to challenge this.

segments.speaker: Pablo Torre
segments.text: Yeah. What you see is that the batter taps his helmet, which is a signal for, I initiate a challenge. I'm taking this to the court of appeals. And, immediately, on the jumbotron, you see the strike zone. And you see the electronic depiction of the ball. And we see that, in fact, the batter was right.

segments.speaker: Commentator
segments.text: ABS powered by T-Mobile-- that's out of the zone! The inning continues!

segments.speaker: Pablo Torre
segments.text: This was not a strike. It was a ball. And the umpire, in other words, has messed up.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And people love it.

segments.speaker: Commentator
segments.text: ABS could be a lot of fun, Mark!

segments.speaker: Pablo Torre
segments.text: I mean, this game becomes this comedic chapter in the history of baseball. Because the very next pitch, another challenge. The batter says, you did it again. J'accuse again.

segments.speaker: Commentator
segments.text: Called strike three, tapped the helmet again.

segments.speaker: Umpire
segments.text: Batter's challengin' the pitch.

segments.speaker: Commentator
segments.text: Here we go.

segments.speaker: Commentator
segments.text: [INDISTINCT CHATTER]

segments.speaker: Commentator
segments.text: [CROWD CHEERING]

segments.speaker: Commentator
segments.text: Outside! The loudest cheers of the game. The Reds have hit two homers, come up back-to-back challenges!

segments.speaker: Pablo Torre
segments.text: And now it's just like you almost begin to feel bad for CB Bucknor, the umpire, almost.

segments.speaker: Commentator
segments.text: Oh, wow.

segments.speaker: Commentator
segments.text: [CROWD CHEERING]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Oh my god. People are standing. They're cheering. People are so excited.

segments.speaker: Pablo Torre
segments.text: It's so great. [LAUGHS] Look, in sports, you dream-- as a sports fan, you dream of stuff like this.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Eugenio Suárez then hit the ball and was tagged out at first. But the Reds won. And-- most eye opening-- the umpire, CB Bucknor, had six of his calls overturned by the robot umpire in that game. That had never happened before in the Major Leagues. Pablo points out Major League Baseball could have gotten rid of the ump at the plate entirely, the way they got rid of line judges in tennis. They could have chosen perfect robot umpiring, perfect calls, balls and strikes like he gasbagged about years ago. But instead, they understood that one of the pleasures of the game is yelling.

segments.speaker: Pablo Torre
segments.text: The fact is that there are few scenarios in American life, or anywhere that I can imagine, where you're empowered. You're legally, contractually allowed to go fucking nuts on the authority figure. Imagine doing that to a judge. You don't get to do that, except in sports.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yeah. There's a quote from the guy who was the chairman of the committee that decided how to roll this out, this guy named John Stanton. And he said that the system that they chose to do retains the human side of the game, quote, "adding a new fan-friendly engagement moment."

segments.speaker: Pablo Torre
segments.text: Yeah. I mean, let's be honest with what that is. A fan-friendly engagement moment is booing the shit out of umpires. That's what fan-friendly engagement means. It means let's give the coliseum some blood.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Now, you and I are talking about this right now because I reached out to you, and I said, we're going to do an episode to commemorate our country's 250th anniversary. And we thought it would be nice to just celebrate and commemorate things that seem very, very American, like, especially American. How does this ABS challenge system fit the bill?

segments.speaker: Pablo Torre
segments.text: Because America, if you're really cutting to the core of us, we want to be mad as much as we want justice. We want to be able to express what's inside of us that feels like it's trapped there as much as we want to see each getting their own fair due. And in this ABS system, what our pastime, our oldest, stodgiest, dustiest pastime has given us is somehow the ability to maybe have both.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Both, meaning we want justice, but we also want to scream at somebody. Hard not to think about what's going on in national politics when he puts it that way. Today on our show, for our July 4 semiquincentennial-- and, yes, I had to look that word up, which means 250th. According to the internet, actually, an alternative word for this is sestercentennial, but that just sounds like a very old nun. For our semiquincentennial, commemorating what this country has been for 250 years, we thought that it would be fun to collect a bunch of things that just seem very particularly American, like changing the rules of our national pastime to allow for more screaming at figures of authority.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Today on our show, we have the most American question, we have a trip to a Michigan sand dune with our own question, and we have so much more. From WBEZ Chicago, it's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. Stay with us.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's This American Life. Our semiquincentennial episode-- boy, that really does not roll off the tongue-- Act One, A Most American Question. So there are definitely are a bunch of questions that Americans have asked over our 250 years that seem very characteristically American. Are you now, or have you ever been, a member of the Communist Party? Do you want fries with that? Where are you from? With its classic companion, where are you really from? One of our contributors, Jiayang Fan, has her pick for the most American question out there.

segments.speaker: Jiayang Fan
segments.text: The first time I heard someone ask the question outside of an ESL class, I was eight years old. Are you OK? I knew so few English words that part of the reason why it registered so distinctly must have been the shock of understanding. Are you OK? A young police officer was asking my mother the question. He had been called, as the police were often called in our first days in America, to our basement apartment.

segments.speaker: Jiayang Fan
segments.text: My mother and I had recently reunited with my father after he'd left to study in America six years earlier. And it hadn't gone well. Doors were slammed, plates shattered, limbs pinned to the ground, ultimatums delivered. Usually, I hid in bed, under the covers, with palms pasted to my ears. But that day, the apartment was quiet. My father had already left for good. Did my mother call because she was being harassed by my father's mistress or because we were being evicted from our basement studio? I no longer remember.

segments.speaker: Jiayang Fan
segments.text: I do remember that it was the first time I dared to look at an American police officer up close-- blue uniform, black boots, a belt heavy and crowded. My mother and I did not look to be in the way of bodily harm. There was nothing more for an officer of the law to do. Are you OK, ma'am?, the man asked as he stood in the doorway. The question hung in the air as a procedural formality, as a way of wrapping up the visit.

segments.speaker: Jiayang Fan
segments.text: I had been in the country for less than a year. But I knew what the next words should be, the standard call and response, the same way that "how are you?" had only one answer. Fine, thank you. How are you? But that day, kneeling on the floor, face covered in her own tears and snot, my mother responded with something else. No, she said. The officer lowered himself onto the floor next to the doorjamb, then listened and nodded for an hour.

segments.speaker: Jiayang Fan
segments.text: I was astonished. My mother followed rules tirelessly and taught me to do the same, all part of adapting as seamlessly as possible. Why would she embarrass herself like that? I didn't understand enough English to follow the conversation, but as I watched my mother closely, I was certain I would never break the script like that.

segments.speaker: Jiayang Fan
segments.text: I spent the next several years irritated with, are you OK? Compelled to be OK with it in public while fuming to my diary in private. Here's an entry from when I was 12. October 26, 1996-- Are you OK? Things going OK, right? Is everything OK? Those are the most common questions in America. I don't like them because they don't tell you anything about anything. Yes! Of course! Great! Those are the most common answers. Isn't that so cheap? I think so. Those questions are so pointless that it is even a waste of words to me.

segments.speaker: Jiayang Fan
segments.text: As I saw it then, the question's hollowness had a distinctly American quality. Here, pleases, thank yous, excuse mes, weren't they always uttered ad nauseam from mouths of people who had already muscled past you? Are you OK was a question, supposedly. But how often was it really a mechanical reflex, an American tic announcing itself? Someone goes down hard in lacrosse practice, and the are you OK? arrives almost simultaneously with the impact. The question is a reflex, not an inquiry.

segments.speaker: Jiayang Fan
segments.text: In our 37 years together, my mother and I were often and unmistakably not OK. Still, it was not a question we often asked of each other. That sort of check-in hit too close to the bone. Not Chinese, my mother would have certainly said, though I never pressed her on it-- also not Chinese.

segments.speaker: Jiayang Fan
segments.text: Lately, though, I've been thinking about the moment she told the police officer she wasn't OK. I thought she flubbed the obligatory call and response of the question. But now I wonder if it was something else. My mother is dead now, but the look on her face as she knelt and cried with a stranger still comes to me sometimes. It arrives most vividly, unbidden, when I'm with friends or mothers, watching their kids on the neighborhood playground.

segments.speaker: Jiayang Fan
segments.text: A scrape on the knee or the elbow, the wound still red and angry, and someone-- a mother, a friend-- administers the question. And there, on the child's open mouth and tears-smeared face, is my mother's shocked look. The child hears the question. It doesn't make the pain go away. But the question stays in the air. It becomes a pause, a door held open.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Jiayang Fan. She's a staff writer at The New Yorker. That story was produced by Diane Wu.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act Two, City on a Hill, of Sand. We here in the land of the free do not like to be told what to do. And additionally, and maybe especially, we don't like to be told what not to do. Aviva DeKornfeld has a story about that very American quality as it plays out in one of our shared public spaces.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: I went to Sleeping Bear Dunes National Lakeshore to see the star attraction, the tallest dune in the park. It's 450 feet high and slopes down at what looks like a 45-degree angle directly into Lake Michigan. If you can't picture 450 feet, imagine a 34-story building. The grade is so steep that from the bottom of the dune, you can't even see up to the top. It's just a wall of sand in front of you.

segments.speaker: Woman 1
segments.text: Oh my gosh.

segments.speaker: Woman 2
segments.text: Be careful.

segments.speaker: Woman 1
segments.text: Good luck.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: All right. Let's get over here. Let's do it. Thank you so much.

segments.speaker: Woman 1
segments.text: Take your time.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: People come from all over the Midwest to walk down this dune and then promptly turn around and trudge right back up. There's only a 2-foot-wide strip of beach at the bottom, so turning around is about all there is to do. This climb is not for everyone. Dozens need assistance climbing out each summer. And because of that, the park service tries to discourage people from climbing the dune without prohibiting it outright.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: They've tried a bunch of different signs. The current one mentions the ecological damage of walking on the dune and says "Down is optional," which is intentionally soft language because their previous signs said that there'd be a $3,000 rescue fee, which Americans seem to take as a kind of personal challenge, and even more people attempted the climb.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Park rangers also patrol the top ridge, asking visitors about their intentions with the dune. Here's Jen, the aggressively mild-mannered ranger on the job today, talking with some prospective climbers.

segments.speaker: Jen
segments.text: It's a lot harder than it looks. I will tell you that.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Oh, I understand that.

segments.speaker: Jen
segments.text: And it's all sand. Yeah, so it is a very challenging climb. Usually, people on the bottom half are using all fours, basically, to get back up. So it's very challenging. But yeah, I think the view is best at the top.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Approximately 8 feet away from Jen sits Jim. He's part of the team of volunteers helping rangers deter people.

segments.speaker: Jim
segments.text: My job up here is to try to save them from themselves, let them know how high this hill is--

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Jim's been volunteering for almost a decade.

segments.speaker: Jim
segments.text: --and the hazards of going--

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: He sits on his chair, wearing his bright orange volunteer vest, pimped out with various pins and patches he's earned over the years, including, proudly, a Junior Ranger badge.

segments.speaker: Jim
segments.text: This is my 86th summer up here.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Oh my gosh.

segments.speaker: Jim
segments.text: Just love it. Yeah.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Wow.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Jim's seen all kinds of ill-advised behavior-- people heading down without water, without shoes, without their inhaler, and worst of all, as far as Jim is concerned, running down the dune.

segments.speaker: Jim
segments.text: We had a girl get badly hurt here. She ran down. She tripped. She vaulted out, tried to stop herself. She dislocated both shoulders, broke a collarbone, wrenched her neck, hurt her back, and cut her head on a rock.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Oh my god.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Standing on the ridge, you can see the slope filled with dozens of people, heads down, slowly, silently trudging up the hill, scores of people who were told not to do this and decided to try it anyway.

segments.speaker: Michael

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: A little further up the hill, I spot another guy named Michael. He's wearing an oversized visor and has blue braces on his teeth. He was part of a whole crew wearing matching hats, celebrating his 50th birthday, if you could call this celebrating.

segments.text: How are you feeling now?

segments.speaker: Mike
segments.text: Tired. Humbling, you know. Every step you take up, you lose at least half of it going backwards, but yeah.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: One guy, who had taken off his sand-filled sneakers and slung them over his neck, kept muttering to himself, like a mantra, I should have listened to my wife. I should have listened to my wife. The reason why you're not hearing that on tape is because it was so hard to move around the dune, zigzagging from person to person.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: [PANTING] Oh my god.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I don't think it's a stretch to say we are a country of people who have been told over and over that we are the exception. So many of our movies, so many of the stories we tell ourselves are about how the rules, the warnings, the statistics, those are for other people. When we hear that most people can't do something, we are trained to think, well, I'm not most people.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But really, when we try to live out this pint-sized American exceptionalism, we are just as likely to find ourselves face down in the sand, panting and humbled, less city on a hill and more bear-crawling up it.

segments.text: I walk over to Jim with my fully-formed kneecaps and pick up our conversation. He started expounding on how he counsels people.

segments.speaker: Jim
segments.text: Well, if I start to tell people about what it's like and-- eagle!

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: A bald eagle flew overhead. We all turned and looked. And there we stood, a bunch of Americans on a perfect summer day, on a dune in a park being destroyed by our actions and maintained by our tax dollars, watching our mascot soar through the sky, indifferent to our plight below.

segments.text: And Survivor is the old-school reality show where they stick a bunch of people on an island and divide them into teams, and they compete in challenges, and then people get voted off, right?

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: Yes. Yes, yes. That's Survivor, classic show. We all know it. And so the season of Survivor I want to talk about is what me, other Survivor fans call the race war season. And we call it that because in this season, they divided the tribes up by race. So there's an African-American tribe. There's a white tribe. There's an Asian-American tribe. There's a Latino tribe. I know that's not a race, but that's how they divided the tribes.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK. So that seems like an incredibly loaded and crazy thing to do. Why did they do this?

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: So basically, Survivor had gotten a lot of criticism because the casting just wasn't very diverse. And on top of that, a lot of times, they would get to the end of the season, and it would only be the white players left.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Oh, the nonwhite players would get voted off early.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: Yes. So this was their response to that. They were like, OK, you guys want more diversity, here is more diversity, which is a choice.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: You have to respect them for kind of doubling down. How did the contestants on the show feel about it?

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: So the contestants seemed kind of confused by it. They're like, why did we make this about race?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Different ethnic groups-- I mean, is that kosher?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: I honestly was stunned. I mean, this was crazy. I mean, on one hand, I think it's a great opportunity because I think it's wonderful that there's more minorities. At the same time, I'm a little bit worried that it might play out to caricatures and stereotypes.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: I remember watching the show and being really shocked when I first started the season because I was like, I can't believe that they did this, but honestly, got over it really quick because basically, something happened in the first season that switched the way I was seeing it. And from there on, it just kept happening.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So what happened?

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: So they start the season in this really dramatic way. They're on a boat in the middle of the South Pacific. And the host, Jeff Probst, is telling all the contestants to gather supplies, get on a raft, and go to shore with your team.

segments.speaker: Jeff Probst
segments.text: They've been given two minutes to salvage whatever they can off this boat.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: And Jeff's like, you have two minutes. Grab as much as you can.

segments.speaker: Jeff Probst
segments.text: You need to catch that chicken. That is food you are going to want.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: So they grab as much as they can, get to the island. And then this thing happens that, really, it could happen on any season of Survivor, which is, someone from one of the tribes steals chickens from the other tribe. But because this season everyone's divided by race, it's like, I kind of can't help but notice that it was the white tribe that stole the chicken from the Asian tribe. And so I'm watching this and I'm thinking, ugh, that is so white. [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I see that.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: But then I'm like, ugh, why did I even think that? Like, looking at my own biases and thinking about how I'm thinking about race, right?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Oh, so you're having this thing where you're finding yourself asking over and over, is that race, or is that me?

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: Yeah. So all that is happening in the first few episodes. And then the producers decide, you know what? Let's end this segregation thing. They're like, mix up the teams. Like, they completely abandoned this initial premise of the season. And everybody is now on integrated teams, basically. But the thing is, because they started out segregated, the race thing is sort of still hanging over the whole thing.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: And then there's this twist that happens. It's right before a challenge. And the two tribes have gathered. And Jeff says, we're going to try something different here.

segments.speaker: Jeff Probst
segments.text: I'm offering each of you the opportunity to mutiny.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: Which essentially means you can abandon your tribe and go and join the other tribe.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And does this play out in a racially charged way?

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: [LAUGHS] Well, the only people who switch are two white players. So they go and join the other white players on the other tribe. And just to say-- they could have done it because they had close relationships with those people, or lots of reasons that they could have done this. But it's hard not to think, watching them walk across to the other side, hmm, white flight.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: Because what it does is it totally creates these two lopsided tribes. So there's one tribe of four left, the tribe they abandoned, which has four POC. And then the other tribe has now eight people-- four white people, two Asian people, one Black person, and one Hispanic person.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And wait. And so one tribe is twice as big as the other. So that must give them an advantage, right?

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: It does in a lot of ways. I think they think, like, oh, we're about to sweep this other tribe. There's no way they're going to win any challenges. And what happens actually is kind of the exact opposite. So the little tribe of four, which is-- they call them the Aitu Four, the little POC coalition-- they basically go on, I would say, one of the greatest runs in Survivor history. So they win every single challenge from then on out, even though they're outnumbered 2 to 1.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: And again, as I'm watching this, it's kind of hard not to think, huh, got to be twice as good, right? It's all these people of color who are having to be smarter and work harder and do all of these things just to stay on the even playing field to win, essentially. And each time they win, the other team has to go to tribal council. They kick off a person of color, until finally, it kind of becomes this very stark thing, where it's down to four white people versus four people of color at the end--

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Oh my god.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: --two alliances.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The producers got what they wanted.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: Kind of. Yeah, right? And then that tribe that is the POC tribe, they keep winning. And then they vote all the white contestants off one by one.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And so when you see how all of this played out by the end of the season, why do you think of this as the most American season of reality TV?

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: Because in general, in this country, we don't want to talk about race. We don't want to have to think about race.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: No, we do not.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: And then we are forced into these situations where we have no choice. We have to talk about it. It's come up again, you guys. Surprise.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yeah. Things happen.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: And then in this season, we have that experience over and over and over again. And to me, it is such a quintessential part of the American experience. And it's all playing out in this game on a frickin' island in the middle of the South Pacific.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Emanuele Berry is the executive editor of our program.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act Four, The Most American Schoolbook. So Roman Mars hosts the podcast 99% Invisible. And he recently started a new series with the BBC. It's called A History of the United States in 100 Objects. And one of the stories on his new show seemed very much in line with what we're talking about here today on our show. It is about a book that shaped education in this country for years. Here's Roman.

segments.speaker: Roman Mars
segments.text: The book I'm going to tell you about was written by one very frustrated schoolteacher. This guy is teaching in 1783. The Revolutionary War is ending, the fighting on American soil finally tapering off. And in every part of regular life, people are trying to figure out, OK, now that we're not British anymore, what does it actually mean to be an American?

segments.speaker: Roman Mars
segments.text: This teacher, he's educating anywhere from 50 to 70 students in a one-room schoolhouse. And these students range from 6 to 16 years old. It's the same in a lot of places around the country. A very small percentage of kids are getting an education. And even if they do get into a classroom, there's no standard curriculum, no shared set of books or processes. The books these students are using are British, teaching British geography, British history, British ways of thinking. People are largely still spelling the word "color" with a U.

segments.speaker: Roman Mars
segments.text: And the schoolteacher, he looks around at all of this and decides, this has to change. His name is Noah Webster.

segments.speaker: Imani Perry
segments.text: He's this person who takes on, as an educator, the problem of literacy.

segments.speaker: Roman Mars
segments.text: That's Imani Perry, author and professor of African-American studies at Harvard University.

segments.speaker: Imani Perry
segments.text: And he complains about the classrooms being crowded and noisy and chaotic. And he is also interested in trying to find a way to standardize American learning.

segments.speaker: Roman Mars
segments.text: So long before his dictionary made him a household name, Webster spends his own money to print a little blue book with an unwieldy title. It's called The First Part of the Grammatical Institute of the English Language, a title so bad that nobody ever used it. They just started calling it the Blue-Back Speller.

segments.speaker: Imani Perry
segments.text: So he really creates this book that is built for an autodidact. It's a way to self-teach. It's not a dictionary. It really is like a guide to learning to read.

segments.speaker: Roman Mars
segments.text: If it sounds kind of counterintuitive that you'd learn to read from a book that requires you to read, here's how that worked. The book contains a bunch of exercises that kind of look like multiplication tables, but with words and letters that you'd memorize. First, you'd start by learning the alphabet-- A, B, C, D. And then you'd move to syllables, like ah, ba, cah, and da, until you finally learn simple words, like bag, big, bog, bug. Eventually, you'd form sentences, read paragraphs. And then you'd read these short stories, a collection of fables and moral parables.

segments.speaker: Roman Mars
segments.text: Webster uses the book to introduce simpler, more distinctly American spellings. He drops the U from humor and labor. He once suggested that we start spelling the word daughter as D-A-W-T-E-R, which would have been nice, though that one didn't stick. But his larger idea does succeed. This book, the Blue-Back Speller, becomes one of the most important books in early America. Entire generations grew up with it.

segments.speaker: Roman Mars
segments.text: At one point, the Blue-Back Speller was second only to the Bible in copies sold. And it also is kind of like a bible. Could you describe its size and the relevance of its size?

segments.speaker: Imani Perry
segments.text: Yeah. It's wonderful to hold one because you realize it's pocket sized. It was small enough to fit into a jacket pocket or pants pocket. It was mobile.

segments.speaker: Roman Mars
segments.text: Yeah. And it could be hidden.

segments.speaker: Imani Perry
segments.text: It could easily be hidden, which was really important.

segments.speaker: Roman Mars
segments.text: Important because it means the book could be used secretly by people who weren't supposed to have it, enslaved people, who were legally prohibited from learning to read. Webster probably never intended this book for Black people at all. While he was against slavery, Webster's books were meant for Americans, who were defined by Webster, in his dictionary, as descendants of Europeans-- white people.

segments.speaker: Imani Perry
segments.text: And despite that fact, his Blue-Back Speller becomes something that is fundamental to African-American struggles for literacy.

segments.speaker: Roman Mars
segments.text: The Blue-Back Speller was everywhere, so common that some enslaved people managed to get their hands on it anyway, even though teaching an enslaved person to read was actually against the law in much of the South.

segments.speaker: Imani Perry
segments.text: Having one of these spellers, for someone who was enslaved, could put you at enormous risk of maiming, of death, of being sold. Black literacy was seen as a threat.

segments.speaker: Roman Mars
segments.text: One of the enslaved people who learned to read this way was Frederick Douglass. He'd go on to become one of the most influential writers and thinkers in American history, an advisor to Abraham Lincoln.

segments.speaker: Imani Perry
segments.text: He and countless other Black people take on that Blue-Back Speller and insist upon becoming part of the literate American public. And one of the early ways we see this is Black soldiers in the Civil War who become literate and immediately begin writing letters to Lincoln, saying not only are they hopeful for land with their freedom, but there have to be schools.

segments.speaker: Roman Mars
segments.text: The Blue-Back Speller found its way from shipyard to town square, from the schoolhouses of New England to the plantations of the South. And when I actually got my hands on it, if I'm being honest, the content of the book itself is kind of a joyless slog. If you asked me to teach someone to read using the Blue-Back Speller, it would be hard. And I can't imagine starting from a place of not being able to read at all and using it to navigate my way to literacy. It just throws you right into the deep end of the pool, swimming in pages of hard-to-navigate tables.

segments.speaker: Roman Mars
segments.text: And then there are the moral parables. They're not exactly compelling and more than a little condescending. If you were someone who didn't get a primary school education, this seems like exactly the kind of book that might put you off of reading forever.

segments.speaker: Roman Mars
segments.text: It takes real conviction to use the book. It goes from basically pre-kindergarten to college inside of a few hundred-- like, maybe a hundred-- no, 200, 150 pages. Let's see. [LAUGHS] Let me look at it.

segments.speaker: Roman Mars
segments.text: It is not something that you just pick up, and all of a sudden you have mastery.

segments.speaker: Imani Perry
segments.text: No. It requires work. And despite that fact, his Blue-Back Speller becomes something that is important. This same object, it's Booker T. Washington and WEB Du Bois for whom the Blue-Back Speller matters. There's something quintessentially American about the Blue-Back Speller. It becomes not only a way to learn to read, but actually, a tool for entry into all kinds of arenas where they had not been contemplated.

segments.speaker: Roman Mars
segments.text: The Blue-Back Speller wasn't what it was because of the genius of Noah Webster. It became what it became because of the people who read it, who made something of it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Roman Mars. A version of this story originally aired on his new show, A History of the United States in 100 Objects. It was originally produced by Priscilla Alabi and aired courtesy of BBC Studios Productions Limited, 99% Invisible, and Sirius XM. You can find the series in the 99% Invisible feed wherever you get your podcasts. Imani Perry tells the story of the Blue-Back Speller in her new book, Black in Blues.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Which brings us to Act 5. Act Five, Jose, Can You See? So one of the areas where this country can really claim to have invented a lot of things is music. There's jazz, there's R&B, there's rock, there's country, there's hip-hop, all created here and then exported around the world. But we do have some musical traditions that are very specific to this country and pretty much have stayed in this country. One of our producers, Emmanuel Dzotsi, has a story about one like that.

segments.speaker: Emmanuel Dzotsi
segments.text: So when I first moved to the US as a kid, years before I became a citizen, I remember noticing this one very distinct thing, which is that every time I saw someone sing the national anthem, they put their own little twist on it. And they always seemed to do it in this one spot.

segments.speaker: Emmanuel Dzotsi
segments.text: ["THE STAR-SPANGLED BANNER" BY WHITNEY HOUSTON] O'er the land of the free

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It doesn't matter the genre of the singer is from.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: ["THE STAR-SPANGLED BANNER" BY RASCAL FLATTS] O'er the land of the free

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And it doesn't matter if they sing the rest of the song fairly straight. People will get to that last part of the song and do something completely different. Sometimes they scat or add their own words.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: ["THE STAR-SPANGLED BANNER" BY STEVE TYLER] O'er the land of the free

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I'm gonna take you there

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: They pull a Mariah Carey because, well, they are Mariah Carey.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: ["THE STAR-SPANGLED BANNER" BY MARIAH CAREY] O'er the land of the free

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This happens so often, I think most Americans have sort of accepted it as a fact. But this sort of thing just doesn't go down like that in other countries. Like, if you take the UK, where I was born, that national anthem--

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: ["GOD SAVE THE KING"] God save our gracious king

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I have no earthly idea where I would even begin to put my own spin on it. The ad-libbing thing is not really something Brits do to "God Save the King," right? Like, you just kind of wish King Charles a happy, victorious life, and you keep it pushing. But when I told some of my coworkers at This American Life about this, they were incredulous. Like, surely, other countries play around with the end of their national anthems. It's the end of a song, dude. Like, what else are you going to do?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I heard all that, and I took it personally. So I set out to prove them wrong. I spoke to five musicologists about this at places like Stanford, Berkeley, UNC. And they all agreed with me. What American singers do at the end of a national anthem is something you really don't see much in other countries. And there are a bunch of reasons for that. Like, for one, Francis Scott Key, who wrote the lyrics to "The Star-Spangled Banner," specifically chose a melody that's designed for showing off. This is very different from other national anthems, which are often marches or hymns.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The tune Scott Key picked came from a musician's club in England and was basically the equivalent of one of those songs you use at a talent show to show your incredible range and voice. In fact, that's why the song is so hard for most of us to sing. The original tune has this kind of "you can't sing with us" energy.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: ["THE ANACREONTIC SONG"] And besides, I'll instruct you, like me, to entwine the myrtle of Venus with a Bacchus's vine

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The other reason other countries don't improvise the way we do on their anthem is-- they don't have our tradition of improvised music. Like, we have jazz, blues, gospel, Black music, where it's built in that you don't always do what's on the page. There's, you know, freedom or whatever, individuality. Duke Ellington did his own version in the 1940s. A newly moved to the US Igor Stravinsky did one too. And yet, the first major recorded instance a vocalist got up at a sporting event and decided they were going to customize "The Star-Spangled Banner" and sing it their own way is relatively recent. The consensus all points to one particular performance of the anthem in 1968.

segments.speaker: Announcer
segments.text: Now, ladies and gentlemen, your attention, please. Please rise and join in the singing of our national anthem.

segments.speaker: Emmanuel Dzotsi
segments.text: It was game 5 of a World Series. And the guy who sang, Jose Feliciano, was a big star. His cover of "Light My Fire" came out that year. And Jose was chosen to do the national anthem that night specifically because of who he was, a young Puerto Rican folk singer who could offer something different. Feliciano doesn't just alter that one line of the song. His version is a whole rethinking of it. It's almost like he's trying to do away with the grandeur of the song and do the opposite, make it intimate.

segments.speaker: Emmanuel Dzotsi
segments.text: ["THE STAR-SPANGLED BANNER" BY JOSE FELICIANO] Whose broad stripes and bright stars

segments.speaker: Emmanuel Dzotsi

segments.speaker: Emmanuel Dzotsi
segments.text: O'er the ramparts we watched

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: A recording Feliciano did of his version was super successful. He opened his concerts with it. And then, a year later, Jimi Hendrix goes even further at Woodstock.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: ["THE STAR-SPANGLED BANNER" BY JIMI HENDRIX]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And a whole raft of people take these big swings. There's Marvin Gaye's 1983 version at the NBA All-Star Game, which sounds like it should come with a free waterbed.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: ["THE STAR-SPANGLED BANNER" BY MARVIN GAYE] Whose broad stripes and bright stars

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Through the perilous fight

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The inspiration for how everybody sings it now, that arrives in 1991, Whitney Houston at the Super Bowl. She slows the song down, changes it from 3/4 time to 4/4 time, which gives her more space. And she sings it mostly straight, until the end and that last line.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: ["THE STAR-SPANGLED BANNER" BY WHITNEY HOUSTON] O'er the land of the free

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And the home of the brave

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: God, I miss Whitney Houston. But yeah, that's how we get to today, a ritual where you, as a vocalist, no matter what your race, what your genre of music, you clock in, do the job you were hired for, sing the song through like they wrote it, and you get two phrases at the end for some real personality. Now, I just want to play you one last version because this weekend, the 250th anniversary of this country, it's probably one of the only appropriate settings for it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This one is the most on the nose, "General Patton in front of the American flag, these colors don't run, if you ain't first, you're last, you can take this anthem from me out of my cold, dead fingers" rendition of "The Star-Spangled Banner" I have yet heard. Because the occasion, I guess, called for it. It was the 100th birthday of the Statue of Liberty, 1986. And the singer was Sandi Patty.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: ["THE STAR-SPANGLED BANNER" BY SANDI PATTY] We look to the stars

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The national anthem normally runs about two minutes. But Sandi, she makes it last for almost six. She adds all these extra verses that were written for the occasion. And every time you think the song's about to end, there is more. I learnt about this version in high school in a music theory class because our teacher used it as the greatest example of key changes. We were still six months away from Beyoncé's "Love on Top." But anyways, Sandi Patty, she takes it higher and higher.
